This result suggests the following elegant outer product representation of any unitary $U$.
Let $\left|v_{i}\right\rangle$ be any orthonormal basis set.
Define $\left|w_{i}\right\rangle \equiv U\left|v_{i}\right\rangle$, so $\left|w_{i}\right\rangle$ is also an orthonormal basis set, since unitary operators preserve inner products.
Note that $U=\sum_{i}\left|w_{i}\right\rangle\left\langle v_{i}\right|$.
Conversely, if $\left|v_{i}\right\rangle$ and $\left|w_{i}\right\rangle$ are any two orthonormal bases, then it is easily checked that the operator $U$ defined by $U \equiv \sum_{i}\left|w_{i}\right\rangle\left\langle v_{i}\right|$ is a unitary operator.

Linear Operators and Matrices\"\n  Excerpt:\n[textbook_2.section.md line 180~180]\n\n### 2.1.2 Linear operators and matrices\n\n\n  New ref: \"Definition 2.1.8\"\n  Excerpt:\n[textbook_2.section.md line 182~196]\n\nA linear operator between vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is defined to be any function $A$ : $V \\rightarrow W$ which is linear in its inputs,\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\nA\\left(\\sum_{i} a_{i}\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right)=\\sum_{i} a_{i} A\\left(\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right) . \\tag{2.10}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nUsually we just write $A|v\\rangle$ to denote $A(|v\\rangle)$.\nWhen we say that a linear operator $A$ is defined on a vector space, $V$, we mean that $A$ is a linear operator from $V$ to $V$.\nAn important linear operator on any vector space $V$ is the identity operator, $I_{V}$, defined by the equation $I_{V}|v\\rangle \\equiv|v\\rangle$ for all vectors $|v\\rangle$.\nWhere no chance of confusion arises we drop the subscript $V$ and just write $I$ to denote the identity operator.\nAnother important linear operator is the zero operator, which we denote 0 .\nThe zero operator maps all vectors to\nthe zero vector, $0|v\\rangle \\equiv 0$.\n\n\n  New ref: \"Definition 2.1.9\"\n  Excerpt:\n[textbook_2.section.md line 200~200]\n\nThen we use the notation $B A$ to denote the composition of $B$ with $A$, defined by $(B A)(|v\\rangle) \\equiv B(A(|v\\rangle))$.\n\n\n  New ref: \"Concept 2.1.10\"\n  Excerpt:\n[textbook_2.section.md line 232~233]\n\nThe matrix whose entries are the values $A_{i j}$ is said to form a matrix representation of the operator $A$.\nThis matrix representation of $A$ is completely equivalent to the operator $A$, and we will use the matrix representation and abstract operator viewpoints interchangeably.\n\n\n  New ref: \"§ 2.1.3.
